source_title: Zagitta/gpu-unlock: Your GeForce runs AI at half speed. This fixes it for 20/30/40 series cards. Up to 2× FP16 / BF16 / TF32 tensor throughput - GitHub
source_excerpt:
Your GeForce runs AI at half speed. This fixes it.
Up to 2× FP16 / BF16 / TF32 tensor throughput · +25–55% LLM prefill · +25–50% fine-tuning · +30–55% image generation
Supported GPUs · Benchmarks · Install · FAQ · Support
NVIDIA ships GeForce cards with their tensor cores capped to half speed for FP16, BF16 and TF32 math with FP32 accumulation, which is what nearly all AI training and unquantized inference uses. The same silicon sold as an RTX A-series or professional card runs at full rate. gpu_unlock removes that cap at boot, before the stock NVIDIA driver loads. No patched driver, no VBIOS flash, nothing to redo when NVIDIA releases a new driver.
Laptops only stay unlocked if the dedicated GPU is never fully powered off. Many laptops power it down when idle, which silently resets the unlock. Turning off runtime power management with options nvidia NVreg_DynamicPowerManagement=0x00 in /etc/modprobe.d/ helps on some models, but expect mixed results.
The exact PCI device IDs are in kernel/gpu_unlock/recipes.c . Linux only. For Windows see the FAQ .
The tensor core rate doubles. How much of that you see depends on how much of your workload is FP16/BF16/TF32 matrix math, and on whether the card has the power headroom to run it.

The RTX 4090 runs out of power before it runs out of tensor cores, so large GEMMs at stock power limits gain much less than the peak rate suggests.
Outputs are bit-identical before and after; only the speed changes. These numbers come from the compatibility reports users have filed, where you can find full benchmark details and post your own.
Then append gpu_unlock.targets=all to your kernel command line, keeping existing options:
GRUB (Debian/Ubuntu/Mint): add it inside GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT in /etc/default/grub , then run sudo update-grub .
GRUB (Arch/CachyOS): same edit, then run sudo grub-mkconfig -o /boot/grub/grub.cfg .
Fedora/RHEL: run sudo grubby --update-kernel=ALL --args="gpu_unlock.targets=all" .
systemd-boot: append it to the options line in your boot entry ( bootctl status shows its location).
UKI / generated entries: add it to /etc/kernel/cmdline and regenerate your boot images/entries (e.g. sudo mkinitcpio -P for mkinitcpio UKIs).
Q: Do you have a website/coin/installer? A: No this is the one and only OG source for gpu-unlock. Crypto, websites, installers and what else is not associated with this project or the developer in any way shape or form.
Q: Does this depend on a specific driver version? I see 610.43.03 is pinned. A: No the driver is only fetched to extract firmware this unlock depends on
Q: What about Windows? A: I don't run windows and don't plan to maintain it but https://github.com/impacifist/Windows-GPU-UNLOCK has built a port, YMMV. There are windows installer's floating around but I would recommend being ++ very ++ careful with those.
Q: What about Blackwell (RTX 50)? A: Not supported and unlikely to happen.
Q: Why did Nvidia handicap my GPU? A: Market segmentation, they want businesses to purchase the professional cards without these limitations at significantly higher prices.
Q: Does this hurt my GPU? A: It's very unlikely, this only unlocks a small handicap Nvidia has put in place to differentiate datacenter and professional cards from consumer versions. It may heat up your GPU slightly because it now does more compute but the standard throttling and power management remains completely intact and should downclock.
Q: How can I assist? A: Please consider donating so I can purchase more GPUs <3
Every build downloads the NVIDIA/CachyOS inputs over HTTPS and generates firmware only in the build directory and the binary package. All three formats install through the same make install-* targets. Packages are built from the working tree, uncommitted changes included.
Build, install build dependencies, and install the packages in one step (asks for your sudo password):
make install uses /etc/os-release ( ID , then ID_LIKE ) to detect Arch, Debian/Ubuntu, or Fedora/RHEL/CentOS families. The RPM installer requires DNF. For other distributions, select a compatible explicit target above.
make arch , make deb and make rpm only build. Debian and RPM packages go to build/deb and build/rpm . The NVIDIA inputs are cached in ~/.cache/gpu-unlock/inputs ( make inputs ; override with INPUTS= ). dpkg-buildpackage itself never uses the network, so a clean-chroot build (sbuild or pbuilder) needs GPU_UNLOCK_INPUTS pointing at that cache. The make dist archive, the Debian source package and the .nosrc.rpm contain no NVIDIA archives or generated firmware.
This Linux kernel module combines the cmpunlocker's V67/PLM technique with the pre-driver timing of the UEFI approach. At boot it runs the unlock, writes the speed selectors (SS0 0x88888888 , which selects the full BF16 rate, and the 4-bit SS1 0x8 IMLA4) and performs an FLR before the unmodified NVIDIA driver binds the card. It is neither a UEFI application nor a patched NVIDIA driver.
The packages put gpu_unlock and its firmware in the initramfs and load it there, before nvidia can bind a card:
mkinitcpio: /etc/mkinitcpio.conf.d/zz-gpu-unlock.conf inserts gpu_unlock right before nvidia in MODULES , so a display card is blank for as short a time as possible. Without nvidia in the image, it goes last and still runs before an nvidia loaded from the root filesystem. Images are rebuilt on install. mkinitcpio ignores drop-ins for an image built with -c or a preset _config ; put gpu_unlock right before nvidia in that config's MODULES yourself.
initramfs-tools: /usr/share/initramfs-tools/modules.d/gpu-unlock.conf .
dracut: /usr/lib/dracut/dracut.conf.d/gpu-unlock.conf .
With initramfs-tools and dracut, the module is built for every installed kernel that has headers, and those kernels' images are rebuilt on install and again on removal. Kernels installed later get the module and a new image from the kernel's own install hooks.
There is no softdep nvidia pre: rule: kmod honours only the first softdep nvidia line it reads, so other packages' rules ( nvidia-utils , gddr6_hwmon ) would silently override it, or it would override theirs.
The module does nothing unless the kernel command line opts in:
Addresses are full PCI names as lspci -D prints them (hex digits in either case), independent of GPU numbering and display role. An entry that is not a supported card (see Supported GPUs ), including all mixed with addresses, is logged and ignored. The cards are unlocked concurrently, about a second in all however many there are, and each on its own: a card that is already bound or powered down is skipped. Bus mastering that the board firmware left on (Supermicro X11 does this whatever its option ROM and bus master settings) is cleared first; a card some driver already initialised is still refused. Then nvidia loads and binds every card as usual.
The display card works too. Its firmware framebuffer (the boot console and Plymouth) keeps running while the unlock's firmware steps run, and is removed just before the card's reset, as nvidia-drm would do a moment later anyway. Its screen is blank from that reset until nvidia-drm takes over.
Loading the module by hand after boot does nothing to a card that nvidia has bound.
Suspend to RAM powers the cards off, which resets the speed selectors. After resume the module unlocks every card it unlocked at boot again, before nvidia resumes it: its suspend notifier runs just ahead of the one nvidia resumes its cards from ( NVreg_UseKernelSuspendNotifiers=1 , the default in current drivers; nvidia-resume.service runs later still). This adds about a second to resume. A card that kept power, as in suspend to idle, is still unlocked and is only read. A card that nvidia has already resumed, or that is bound to another driver, is left as it is, and the log says why. Add gpu_unlock.resume=0 to the kernel command line, or write 0 to /sys/module/gpu_unlock/parameters/resume , to turn this off. Hibernation is not covered.
To stop unlocking, remove gpu_unlock.targets= from the kernel command line; for a one-off boot, delete it in the bootloader's edit screen. Removing the packages also removes the module and the initramfs drop-ins.
If the firmware on a card never stops, the module logs it and keeps the DMA buffers that firmware may still use until the next power off. Power off before trying again.
The kernel module and local packaging are GPL-2.0-only. The generated buffer derives from the pinned CMP reference; NVIDIA firmware remains under its own terms. See firmware/NOTICE.md and licenses/ for attribution and notices.
